meta.audience: The people of Zarahemla, Jershon, and Gideon
meta.location: Zarahemla, Jershon, Gideon, and among the Zoramites
principles: Belief outside the reach of law
Evidence and the demand for a sign
A teacher believing his own case

world_behind.title: The dead of the last war went uncounted
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says neither side's dead could be numbered. Alma 28 gave the mourning; this chapter opens by admitting the arithmetic failed.

world_behind.title: Nephite law protected belief
world_behind.text: Verses 7 through 11 state the rule at length: crimes were punished and belief was not, because a law over belief would put men on unequal ground. Mormon explains the legal setting before he introduces the man it protected.

world_behind.title: Korihor could not be prosecuted
world_behind.text: Verse 12 says the law could have no hold on him. Everything that happens to him afterward comes from the people he preached to, not from a court.

world_behind.title: Nehor had made the same move a generation earlier
world_behind.text: Alma 1 has a man preaching for gain and money, and Korihor accuses the priests of exactly that. The charge of glutting on the people's labor is the book's recurring complaint against religion.

world_behind.title: Two communities threw him out
world_behind.text: Jershon bound him and carried him to Ammon; Gideon bound him and took him to Giddonah and the chief judge. Mormon calls the people of Ammon more wise than many of the Nephites.

world_behind.title: Alma answers the money charge with his own accounts
world_behind.text: Verses 32 and 33 have him say he worked with his own hands from the start of the reign of the judges and never took a senine for church labor. Alma 11 had already priced a senine.

world_behind.title: The Zoramites appear at the end
world_behind.text: Verse 59 introduces them as people who separated from the Nephites under a man named Zoram, and Korihor dies among them. Alma 31 opens on that field.

words.text: One who stands against Christ. The record uses the hyphenated form twice, both in this chapter, and the King James Bible spells it without the hyphen in the letters of John, where many antichrists are already at work (1 Jn. 2:18). Mormon applies it to a man whose whole case is that there is nothing to be against.

Disorder of the mind. The word occurs once in scripture. Korihor uses it as a diagnosis: a remission of sins is a frenzied mind's effect, produced by inherited tradition. He is arguing that belief is a medical condition.

To gorge, to feed to excess. The record uses it three times and the King James Bible never; Mosiah 9 has Lamanites wanting to glut themselves on the labors of Zeniff's people. Korihor turns the word on Nephite priests, and Alma answers it with a wage statement.

Passing fancies. The word appears once in scripture, in a list Korihor builds out of traditions, dreams, whims, visions, and pretended mysteries. The list is the chapter's sharpest piece of writing, and it belongs to the man being refuted.

The smallest gold measure in the Nephite system. Alma 11 sets it equal to a judge's daily wage and to a senum of silver. Alma says he has never received one for church labor, which converts his denial into an exact figure his hearers could price.

Unable to speak. Treated at Mosiah 14:7. It appears thirteen times in the record, and the King James Bible twenty-nine. Zacharias is struck dumb in Luke 1 for disbelieving a promise; Korihor is struck dumb for demanding a sign, and the sign he gets is the silence.

phrases.term: There was no law against a man's belief
phrases.text: Mormon states the constitutional position before the trial begins. A law reaching belief would put men on unequal ground, which he says is strictly contrary to the commands of God.

phrases.term: All men were on equal grounds
phrases.text: The reason the protection exists. Punishment attaches to acts, and acts alone, so that no one starts at a disadvantage. Mormon repeats the point twice in five verses.

phrases.term: Ye cannot know of things which ye do not see
phrases.text: Korihor's central claim, and it is a claim about knowledge rather than about God. Everything else he says depends on it, and Alma's answer in verse 44 attacks it directly.

phrases.term: Every man fared in this life according to the management of the creature
phrases.text: Korihor's whole doctrine in one clause: people get what they manage to get. Prosperity follows genius, victory follows strength, and no act is a crime. Mormon reports it as a summary rather than a quotation.

phrases.term: They were more wise than many of the Nephites
phrases.text: Mormon's assessment of the people of Ammon, who bound Korihor and removed him. Converted Lamanites handle the Anti-Christ better than the nation that has had the record for six hundred years.

phrases.term: Ye say that this people is a free people. Behold, I say they are in bondage
phrases.text: Korihor's rhetorical method, used four times running. He restates the priest's position and reverses it, and the pattern gives his speech its momentum without adding evidence.

phrases.term: A being who never has been seen or known, who never was nor ever will be
phrases.text: The end of Korihor's list, and the strongest thing he says. He is accusing the priests of inventing an accountability that keeps people from enjoying their own property.

phrases.term: I have never received so much as even one senine for my labor
phrases.text: Alma's answer to the charge of gain, given as an accounting. He names the exception honestly: judges are paid according to law for their time. The defense is specific enough to be checked.

phrases.term: All things denote there is a God
phrases.text: Alma's counter to the demand for a sign. He offers his brethren's witness, the prophets, the scriptures, the earth, its motion, and the planets moving in regular form. The argument is that evidence is already everywhere.

phrases.term: I do not deny the existence of a God, but I do not believe that there is a God
phrases.text: Korihor's last spoken sentence, and it gives away more than he meant. He has moved from certainty to a statement about his own belief, and Alma strikes him dumb one verse later.

phrases.term: I always knew that there was a God
phrases.text: Written, not spoken, after the sign. Korihor says the devil appeared as an angel, taught him what to say, and that he taught it until he believed it himself. The confession explains how a man argues himself into his own case.

verses.label: v. 7–11
verses.title: Five verses of jurisprudence before the antagonist speaks
verses.text: The record sets out the legal frame first, and grounds it in a principle and not a policy: a law touching belief would put men on unequal grounds, which is contrary to the commands of God. Then it lists what the law does reach, four crimes stacked into verse 10: murder, robbery, theft, adultery. Only after the rule and its exceptions are established does Korihor appear.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: The decisive legal point is put in brackets
verses.text: "(And the law could have no hold upon him)" is not spoken by anyone. It is the record stepping in mid-sentence to state the consequence of the five verses just laid down, in a parenthesis, before the preaching starts. Helaman 2:8 uses the same device to name a conspiracy the story has no word for yet.

verses.label: v. 52–53
verses.title: The confession includes becoming his own convert
verses.text: What Korihor writes is not only that the devil taught him what to say, but what happened afterwards: he taught it because it pleased the carnal mind, had much success, "insomuch that I verily believed that they were true." The record has him report that he ended up persuaded by his own preaching, and it puts that after the admission of where the material came from.

verses.label: v. 55
verses.title: The mercy is refused, and the reason is given aloud
verses.text: Alma does not pray for the curse to be lifted, and says why: "thou wouldst again lead away the hearts of this people." He then hands the outcome off rather than closing it, "it shall be unto thee even as the Lord will." The record prints a prophet declining a request and reasoning from consequences.

chapter.title: The chapter is built as a legal brief
chapter.text: Six verses on why belief cannot be prosecuted come before the man arrives. Mormon wants the reader to know that everything Korihor said was lawful, and that the response had to be argument.

chapter.title: His case rests on a rule about knowledge
chapter.text: You cannot know what you have not seen. Alma's reply widens what counts as seeing to include the earth, its motion, and the planets, which is a disagreement about evidence rather than about faith.

chapter.title: The economic charge is the one Alma answers in detail
chapter.text: He gives three verses to wages and one sentence to metaphysics. The accusation that could be checked is the one he checks.

chapter.title: Converted Lamanites handle him best
chapter.text: Three receptions are reported in three verses. Jershon binds him at verse 20 and the record supplies a comparative verdict in the same clause, "they were more wise than many of the Nephites." Gideon binds him at verse 21, where "he did not have much success." Zarahemla, at verses 12 through 18, lets him preach at length and the record quotes six verses of it. The group that handles him fastest is the one converted most recently, and the record says so rather than leaving it to be inferred.

chapter.title: He asks for a sign and is refused twice before he gets one
chapter.text: Alma says the testimony already available should be enough, warns him of the consequence, and then delivers it. The sign is a punishment that works by taking away his instrument.

chapter.title: The confession explains self-deception
chapter.text: Verse 52 has him write two things at once, "I know that nothing save it were the power of God could bring this upon me" and "I always knew that there was a God." Verse 53 supplies the sequence, that he was taught "even until I had much success, insomuch that I verily believed that they were true." The record thus reports a man persuaded by his own case, and puts the confession in writing because verse 50 has taken his speech away.

chapter.title: Mercy is refused on grounds of consequence
chapter.text: Alma will not ask for the curse to be lifted because Korihor would resume. The chapter leaves the outcome to the Lord and records the reasoning without softening it.

chapter.title: The Zoramites walk on at the last minute
chapter.text: Korihor dies among a people the reader has not met, named in the final verses. The chapter ends by handing its own conclusion to the next mission.

applications.title: Protect the belief you disagree with
applications.text: Nephite law made no offence of belief, and the record gives the reason, that a law bringing men "on to unequal grounds" was "strictly contrary to the commands of God." Punishment attached only to acts: murder, robbery, theft, adultery. Sort what you are objecting to into what somebody thinks and what somebody did.

applications.title: Notice when a claim is about knowledge
applications.text: Korihor's argument turns on what anyone could know rather than on what God is like: "no man can know of anything which is to come," and "ye cannot know that there shall be a Christ." An argument about the limits of knowing needs a different answer from an argument about the facts.

applications.title: Look at what the doctrine licensed
applications.text: The record reports the effect alongside the claim: people lifting up their heads in wickedness, and being led "to commit whoredoms." A belief has practical consequences, and watching them is fair evidence about it.

applications.title: Answer the checkable charge
applications.text: Accused of living off the people, Alma answers with his own record, "I have labored even from the commencement of the reign of the judges until now, with mine own hands for my support." When the accusation is factual, answer it with facts before answering anything else.

applications.title: Refuse the sign, then say what already counts as one
applications.text: Alma declines to produce a sign and lists what is already available, "all things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it." Ask what evidence you have been walking past while asking for a different kind.

applications.title: Watch what repetition does to you
applications.text: He taught what people wanted to hear "even until I had much success, insomuch that I verily believed that they were true." Saying a thing often enough is a way of coming to believe it, and the chapter names that mechanism outright.

applications.title: Decline to undo the consequence
applications.text: Alma refuses to lift the curse and gives the reason, "thou wouldst again lead away the hearts of this people." Mercy that would restore somebody's capacity to do the same damage is questionable mercy, and the chapter lets the refusal stand.

applications.title: Notice where the argument went next
applications.text: Korihor ends among the Zoramites, and Alma 31 opens with Alma going after them. The record does not treat the debate as won when the debater falls; it follows the idea to where it landed.

questions.text: Where do I want a rule that would punish what someone thinks?
What part of me agrees that people mostly get what they manage to get?
When did I last remove something harmful instead of arguing with it?
Could I answer a charge about my motives with specifics?
What denotes to me that there is a God, and when did I last look at it?
What have I said out loud that was stronger than what I actually believe?
What am I repeating because it goes over well?
